blocks.text: Did Subash Chandra Bose really die in a plane crash on August 18th, 1945? Or was India told a story that was never properly proven? Every year on the day Bose supposedly died, Prime Minister Modi post nothing. No tribute, no mention, nothing.  Why? There must be a strong reason. Most people know the ending. A plane crashes in Taiwan. Bose suffers severe burns and dies. But here's where it gets strange. No Japanese, British or Indian government ever filed an official death record for Bose. Now remember one name,

Ichiro Okura, a soldier who died same week. And unlike Bose, his death left a paper trail. That detail becomes important later. Because by the end, you'll see what the records actually say about August 18th, 1945, and why 81 years later, India's most powerful leaders still say nothing. So what actually happened in August 1945? Japan is losing the war. This is the same war that turned Bose from a

political leader into an army commander. The US has just dropped nuclear bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki. His army built from prisoners of war and plantation workers is starving in Burma. Japan armed them then  abandoned them. Bose is trapped in Saigon. He's the leader with no country left. The British are closing in. If he surreners, they will hang him for treason. His own men are already on trial for war crimes back in Delhi. So he does something nobody expects. Instead of giving himself up or

ending his own life, he decides to disappear and start over somewhere else. On August 15th, his cabinet meets one last time  and agrees he should try reach Soviet Russia. He heads north towards Manuria towards the only power left that might take him in. Back home, nobody knows any of this. To India, Naji is still marching, still winning. That belief has about 72 hours left to live. On August 17th, both said goodbye to most of his men at Saigon airfield. The

Japanese tell him  there is only one more seat on the plane. He picks one man, Habibu Rahman. The rest of his staff are left behind in Saigon. He climbs onto an overloaded Japanese bomber. There is no seat left for him either. So he sits on the floor with the fuel tank against his back. One other man on that flight matters. Lieutenant General Shidi Sununamasa, a senior Japanese officer traveling north for his own reasons. That night, the plane stops at Terrain. The next morning, August 18th, it lands at Taipei. That

afternoon, 2 p.m. at the military airfield in Taipei, Taiwan. The plane reportedly crashes on takeoff. Within hours, a hospital reports Bose dead of thirdderee burns. Within a week, its front page news across  India. Na gi is dead. Rahman survives badly burned. For next 60 years, his account is the only eyewitness story anyone has. The entire official version rests on his word alone. But Rahman isn't the only one who claims to have seen it happen.

Look at what other witnesses say. Habibu Rahman said plane barely left the ground. Shiro Nunogaki said the plane split in two. Makato Yamamoto said it never broke apart at all. Even the time of Bosa's death moves from witness to witness. 5:00 p.m. 7:00 p.m. 9:00 p.m. 11:00 p.m. almost midnight. These are not different memories of the same event. These are different men, each unsure of the same false story. Lieutenant General Sunsar is reported dead in the same crash. No Japanese record of his death ever turns up

either. A simple story or it seems because every single thing that should happen next doesn't. No Japanese officer ever files a crash report. Even though the crash reportedly killed a general and a head of a state, no Taiwanese newspaper reports his death, not even the one that writes about Bos's own family few weeks later. Bose is one of the most famous revolutionaries in Asia, and nobody writes a word. Yet, when news finally reaches India days later, it lands like a shock wave. Shops shut down, crowds gathering in streets,

refusing to believe it. Some openly saying their leader cannot be dead. Even Nu doesn't investigate.  In private, he admits the news feels almost like a relief. Gandhi says he feels like in his gut Bose is alive, but he never checks. The British aren't fully sure either. Privately, their own file showed doubt whether Bose is really dead. That doubt is one of the reason they rush to try captured soldiers for treason in Delhi. Before public doubt in his death can turn into public sympathy for his men. Remember that the two biggest

leaders in free India and neither one asks a single hard question. Everyone is too busy grieving to ask the question that should have kept the case open. One man refuses. Bose's own brother Sur. But someone else also goes looking. In August 1946, an Indian journalist named Harin Sha travels to Taipei on his own to find proof. A Taiwanese nurse tells him she personally cared for dying Bose. Health officials hand him a cremation permit and hospital reports for the body. Sha comes home convinced Bose is

dead. His own editor isn't impressed, telling him plainly, "If you say he's dead, it is no news." Sha sits on a story for 10 years. In 1956, Sha finally published his own account as a book. Around the same time, the government holds its first inquiry, the Shaavas committee. Under Prime Minister Neu, it leaned on Rahman's word and Sha's new book and rules that Bose died in the crash. But one committee member refuses to sign off. Bose's brother writes his own dissenting report accusing the committee of choosing politics over evidence. He asks a question that India

will spend next 60 years, three commissions  and tens of thousands of pages trying to answer. What if the crash was staged not to kill Bose but to save him? Either he died on that runway or the whole story is a coverup. feels like it has to be one or the other, right?  It isn't. One story ends here. A much bigger one is just starting. If this story was already this full of holes, why did the truth take another 50 years to surface? Neu's own intelligence bureau had quietly removed pages from

the evidence file before that first committee even began work. 14 years later, a second commission opens under Prime Minister  Indra Gandhi, the Kosla Commission. Reporting in 1974, Justice Kosla goes back to Harin Sha's evidence and this is where it falls apart. The nurse Sha wrote about Sanp Sha never existed.  Hospital record shows only male nurses worked there in 1945. A photograph in Sha's book shown to caretaker's son is denied by him, not his father. And the

cremation permit and hospital reports Sha had given never carried Naji's name at all. They belong to a Japanese soldier called Ichiro  Okura who died of heart failure on August 19th. One day after the crash at the same hospital, Kosla still rules that Bose died. He just can no longer say Sha's evidence proves it. Then a Kolkata High Court order forced a third commission in 1999 set up by the BJPled government at the center and led by a retired Supreme Court judge  with nothing left to lose. Justice Manoj

Mukharji. For the first time, an Indian  investigator isn't looking for confirmation. He's looking for proof. He runs into a problem right away. The government stalls him. For decades, ashes kept at Trancoji Temple in Japan were treated as Naji's remains, but they can't be tested. Boza's own wife spent her life refusing to believe they were his. Where his grand nephew smuggles out a fragment  for secret testing, the sample breaks down before anyone gets a clear answer. Dead end after dead end until Mukherji  tries one place no Indian investigator had ever

seriously searched.  Taiwan's own municipal archives. In March 2005, Taiwanese officials handed him something no British, Japanese or Indian investigators had ever seen before. The original 1945 cremation and death registers. For that exact week, 60-year-old paperwork the Japanese government had always claimed no longer existed. There is no entry of Subhashundra. There is an entry for Ichiro Okura died of heart failure. Cremated 3 days later, same crematorium, same doctor who once claimed to have

treated Bose personally. His paperwork survived.  Naji's paperwork never existed at all. Taiwan's own records confirm what Kosla had already suspected 30 years earlier. Neither  Bose nor anyone else from that crash was actually cremated in Taipei that week. Mukerji's conclusion delivered in November 2005 is blunt. The missing cremation entry defeats the story of his death. The crash he ruled was almost certainly staged by Japanese military and Bose's  own aid to cover an

escape towards Soviet territory. 60 years of official history fell apart in one paragraph. So does that finally answer where Bose went? No. It answers something smaller and almost as important. It proves the country was lied to. This moment doesn't get a parade or a headline. It gets quiet report sitting in an archive saying the story an entire country grew upon was never true. That should have been end of it. It wasn't.

So the truth gets found. Does the government finally admit it? No. In May 2006 under Prime Minister Manm Singh, Parliament rejected Mukharji's findings outright without an explanation. The government that had set  up the commission had changed by the time the report arrived and the new one wasn't ready to undo decades of official history that easily. The truth isn't lost anymore. It's just filed away again.  What follows isn't one big reveal. It's 20 years of steady pressure from researchers who call themselves mission naji. Using India's

new right to information law to force open files that were never meant to be opened. By 2012, over thousand government files, the biggest release of Bose related records in Indian history arrived at national archives. What's in them is almost harder to accept than the coverup itself. For more than two decades after independence, India's own government secretly monitored Bose's family and opened his widow's letters. Then this officials were sharing intelligence on their own martyr with Britain's MI5, the very colonial power he spent his life fighting. On January

23rd, 2016, Naki's birthday, Prime Minister Modi personally released the first 100 files, roughly 15,000 pages to the public. It's a real step towards transparency. It confirms the surveillance. It confirms that even inside the government, officials never fully believed their own story, but it isn't the whole truth. The core intelligence files from India's intelligence bureau and its foreign intelligence wing are still classified today. Nothing explains why a free democratic India would spy on a dead hero's family for 20 straight years

unless somewhere in its own file it never actually believed he was dead. So here's the real question. If Bose did not die on that runway, what actually happened to him that night? Look at this chart. It's a timeline of every official inquiry into Bose's death starting from the same year he vanished in November 1945. Just 3 months later, British intelligence officer filed a report that quoted a Japanese interpreter Watanabi who said plainly that Bose had been sent north towards Russia. This was not some theory invented by researchers 60 years

later. The British intelligence was already saying it within weeks. So where did he actually go? Other declassified files tried to answer that. A wartime intercept from August 18th, 1945 shows Japan's own government telling Tokyo that Bose had already set off by air for Manuria to reach the Soviets. A Soviet document found in 1996 records a 1946 meeting of Soviet leaders discussing what to do with Bose. It places him in Siberia. Even later, India's own ambassador in Moscow is said to have

quietly seen Bose held there. A German prisoner claimed  he met Bose in a Siberian camp in 1948. But none of this evidence was enough for government to agree  that Bose did not die in that plane crash. It may be why India's own government still will not open its last files on Bose. Not because he is a myth, because somewhere in those files, there may be an answer nobody in power wants to give.
